title: Words You Can't Take Back
excerpt: Words can give life or wound deeply. Proverbs on the tongue, gentle answers, and the grace for the words you can't take back.

blocks.text: You know the silence.

It comes right after you say the thing. The sentence is already out of your mouth, already in the air, already landing on the face of the person you said it to. You watch it hit. And in that half-second, every part of you scrambles to reach out and pull it back, the way you'd grab a glass sliding off a counter.
But you can't. Words don't work that way. Once they leave, they're gone, and all that's left is the silence and the look on their face.

Most of us have been on both sides of that moment. We've said the thing, and we've been the one it was said to. And if we're honest, we can still replay a few of those sentences, word for word, years later. The ones that cut us have a way of staying with us longer than almost anything else.
The book of Proverbs understood this better than we do. It spends an unusual amount of time on speech, and it doesn't treat it as a matter of manners. It treats it as a matter of life and death.
More Than Manners

verses: The tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it will eat its fruit.

blocks.text: That's not a poetic exaggeration. Think about what words have actually done in your life. A teacher who said you were capable, and you believed her for decades. A parent's offhand comment you've never quite shaken. The sentence that ended a friendship. The sentence that started a marriage. We tend to treat words as light, quick, disposable things. Proverbs says they're closer to seeds. Whatever you plant, you eat from.

Look at how the book describes the two extremes. On one side: "The words of the reckless pierce like swords" (12:18). Notice the word *reckless*. It doesn't say malicious. Most of the damage we do with our mouths isn't planned. It's the joke that went too far, the thing said in the heat of the moment, the careless comment we didn't think twice about. We didn't mean it that deeply. They felt it that deeply.

And on the other side, in the very same verse: "but the tongue of the wise brings healing." Healing. As though a sentence could do the work of medicine. And apparently, it can. "Gracious words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones" (16:24). You've probably felt this too: the encouragement that got you through a week, the apology that finally lifted something heavy, the "I'm proud of you" you didn't know you needed.
The same small muscle can do both. That's the sobering part.
The Smallest Advantage in an Argument
If you want to see Proverbs at its most practical, try this one:

verses: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.

blocks.text: There's a quiet kind of wisdom in that. Anger feeds on anger. If someone raises their voice at you, every instinct says to raise yours back, and for a moment it even feels justified. But a gentle answer refuses to feed the fire. It doesn't mean you're weak or that you agree. It means you've decided that winning the moment isn't worth losing the person.

Anyone who has tried this knows how hard it is. It takes more strength to soften your voice when you're angry than to sharpen it. But watch what happens when you do it. Often the whole temperature of the room changes. You didn't win an argument. You may have saved a relationship.
The Wisdom of Saying Less
Here is one of the most countercultural lines in the whole book:

verses: Sin is not ended by multiplying words, but the prudent hold their tongues.

blocks.text: We live in a world that rewards the quick response. The fast take, the instant reply, the comment typed before the thought is finished. We've built entire platforms around the idea that having an opinion immediately is a virtue. Proverbs suggests that the more we talk, the more chances we give ourselves to say something we'll wish we hadn't.

That doesn't mean silence is always right. There are times to speak up, and Proverbs says that too. But it does mean there's a skill most of us never learned: the pause. The breath before the reply. The question, *Is this true? Is this kind? Does this need to be said by me, and does it need to be said right now?*
If you take only one thing from this post, let it be that pause. It's small. It's almost embarrassingly simple. And it will prevent more regret than almost anything else you could practice.
But What About the Words You Already Said?

This is where I think a lot of us get stuck. It's all well and good to talk about future words. But what about the ones already out there? The things you said to your child in a moment of frustration. The text you sent that you can't unsend. The thing you said about someone behind their back. The cruel line you delivered because you knew exactly where it would hurt.
Proverbs can't fix that. It can only show you the problem, and maybe that's why it leaves you with an ache. We recognize ourselves in the "reckless" and we know we've done damage we can't undo.

This is where the gospel steps in. The Bible has a startling way of describing who Jesus is: "In the beginning was the Word... and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:1, 14). God's own Word, His final and fullest message to us, arrived in a person.

And look at what that Word did with His own mouth. When He was insulted, Scripture says, "he did not retaliate" (1 Peter 2:23). He was mocked, lied about, spat on, and told to prove Himself, and He answered with a restraint that none of us could manage on our best day. The One whose words created the universe held His tongue when it would have been completely justified to speak.

And then He did something more. He carried the weight of every word we've regretted, every cruel thing, every careless thing, every lie, to the cross. The writer of Hebrews says His blood "speaks a better word" than any accusation against us (Hebrews 12:24). The words we can't take back have been answered by a Word that can't be taken away.

That doesn't erase the need to make things right. If you owe someone an apology, go and give it. But you don't go carrying the full weight of the thing yourself. "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us" (1 John 1:9). Even the sentences you wish you could unsay.
Starting Over, One Sentence at a Time

So here's what I'd leave you with. Before your next conversation, before your next reply, before the next time you feel the heat rising in your chest, try the pause. Let the Spirit of the One who spoke life into you shape what comes out of your mouth next. Ask for words that heal instead of pierce. Let your answers be gentle, even when the other person's aren't. And when you fail, as you will, come back to the Word who didn't fail on your behalf.
You can't take back the words you've said. But you can choose the next ones. And you're not choosing them alone.

Lord Jesus, You know every word I've said that I wish I could take back, and You know the ones still sitting in my heart that I haven't said. Forgive me. Heal what I've broken. Teach me to pause before I speak, to answer gently, and to use my words to build up instead of tear down. Let what comes out of my mouth reflect the grace You've shown me. Amen.
